readings.c1s1:
¶
'''unwarily''' (un-wā′ri-li), ''adv.'' In an unwary manner; without vigilance and caution; heedlessly; unexpectedly. ''Shak.'', K. John, v. 7. 63.

'''unwariness''' (un-wā′ri-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unwary; want of caution; carelessness; heedlessness; recklessness.

'''unwarlike''' (un-wâr′līk), ''a.'' Not warlike; not fit for war; not used to war; not military.
{{smaller block|The ''unwarlike'' disposition of Ethelwolf gave encouragement, no doubt, and easier entrance to the Danes.
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., v.}}}}

'''unwarm''' (un-wârm′), ''v. i.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''warm.''] To lose warmth; become cold. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|With horrid chill each little heart ''unwarms.'' {{right|''Hood.''}}}}

'''unwarned''' (un-wârnd′), ''a.'' Not warned; not cautioned; not previously admonished of danger. ''Locke.''

'''unwarnedly''' (un-wâr′ned-li), ''adv.'' Without warning or notice. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|They be suddenly and ''unwarnedly'' brought forth.
{{right|''Bp. Bale'', Select Works, p. 88.}}}}

¶
'''unwarp''' (un-wârp′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''warp.''] To reduce from the state of being warped. ''Evelyn.''

'''unwarped''' (un-wârpt′), ''a.'' Not warped; not biased; impartial; unbiased. ''Thomson,'' Spring.

'''unwarrantability''' (un-wor″a̤n-tạ-bil′ị-ti), ''n.'' The character of being unwarrantable; unwarrantableness.

'''unwarrantable''' (un-wor′a̤n-tạ-bl), ''a.'' Not warrantable; not defensible; not justifiable; illegal; unjust; improper. ''South,'' Sermons.

'''unwarrantableness''' (un-wor′a̤n-tạ-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unwarrantable. ''Bp. Hall,'' Ans. to Vind. of Smectymnuus, § 3.

'''unwarrantably''' (un-wor′a̤n-tạ-bli), ''adv.'' In an unwarrantable manner; in a manner that cannot be justified. ''Bp. Hall.''

'''unwarranted''' (un-wor′a̤n-ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not warranted; not authorized; unjustifiable: as, an ''unwarranted'' interference.
{{smaller block|What do we weaklings so far presume upon our abilities or success as that we dare thrust ourselves upon temptations unbidden, ''unwarranted.''
{{right|''Bp. Hall,'' Contemplations, iv. 221.}}}}
'''2.''' Not guaranteed; not assured or certain.
{{smaller block|Upon hope of an ''unwarranted'' conquest. {{right|''Bacon.''}}}}
'''3.''' Not guaranteed to be good, sound, or of a certain quality: as, an ''unwarranted'' horse.

¶
{{smaller block|Whan thei han eten, thei putten hire Dissches ''unwasschen'' in to the Pot or Cawdroun, with remenant of the Flessche and of the Brothe, til thei wole eten azen.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 250.}}}}

'''unwasted''' (un-wās′ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not wasted or lost by extravagance; not lavished away; not dissipated.—'''2.''' Not consumed or diminished by time, violence, or other means. ''Sir R. Blackmore.''—'''3.''' Not devastated; not laid waste.
{{smaller block|The most southerly of the ''unwasted'' provinces.
{{right|''Burke'', Nabob of Arcot’s Debts.}}}}
'''4.''' Not emaciated, as by illness.

'''unwatchful''' (un-woch′fu̇l), ''a.'' Not vigilant. ''Jer. Taylor'', Sermons, II. 20.
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''unwatchfulness''' (un-woch′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unwatchful; want of vigilance. ''Leighton'', Com. on 1 Pet. iii.

'''unwater''' (un-wâ′tėr), ''v. t.'' In ''mining'', to free, as a mine, of its water by draining, pumping, or in any other way. ''Encyc. Brit.'', XVI. 457.

'''unwatered''' (un-wâ′tėrd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Freed from water; drained, as a mine.—'''2.''' Not watered; undiluted; unmoistened.—'''3.''' Not supplied with water; not given water to drink.

'''unwatering''' (un-wâ′tėr-ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''unwater'', ''v.''] The act or process of taking water from anything; draining; drainage. ''The Engineer'', LXVII. 298.

'''unwavering''' (un-wā′vėr-ing), ''a.'' Not wavering; not unstable; not fluctuating; fixed; constant; steadfast. ''Strype'', Eccles. Mem., Edw. VI., an. 1551.

'''unwaveringly''' (un-wā′vėr-ing-li), ''adv.'' In an unwavering manner; steadfastly.

'''unwayed†''' (un-wād′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unwaied''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wayed''.] '''1.''' Not used to the road; unaccustomed to the road.
{{smaller block|Colts ''unwayed'' and not used to travel. {{right|''Suckling.''}}}}
'''2.''' Having no roads; pathless.
{{smaller block|It [the land] shal be ''vnwaied'' or wayles.
{{right|''Wyclif'', Ezek. xiv. 15.}}}}

'''unweakened''' (un-wē′knd), ''a.'' Not weakened; not enfeebled. ''Boyle.''

'''unweaned''' (un-wēnd′), ''a.'' Not weaned; hence, not withdrawn or disengaged.
{{smaller block|The heathen Angle and Saxon, still ''unweaned'' from his fierce Teutonic creed. ''E. A. Freeman'', Amer. Lects., p. 128.}}
readings.c2s2:
¶
'''unweariable''' (un-wē′ri-a̤-bl), ''a.'' That cannot be tired out or wearied. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, i. 4.

'''unweariably''' (un-wē′ri-a̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an unweariable manner; indefatigably. ''Bp. Hall'', Christian Assurance of Heaven.

'''unwearied''' (un-wē′rid), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not wearied; not fatigued.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''unwearied'' sun from day to day
Does his creator’s power display.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', Ode.}}}}
'''2.''' Indefatigable; assiduous: as, ''unwearied'' perseverance: of persons.
{{smaller block|<poem>Would you leave me
Without a farewell, Hubert? fly a friend
''Unwearied'' in his study to advance you?</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Beggars’ Bush, i. 2.}}}}

'''unweariedly''' (un-wē′rid-li), ''adv.'' In an unwearied manner; indefatigably; assiduously. ''Chesterfield.''

'''unweariedness''' (un-wē′rid-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unwearied. ''Baxter.''

'''unweary<sup>1</sup>''' (un-wē′ri), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unwery'', < AS. ''unwērig'', not weary; as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''weary''.] Not weary.
{{smaller block|I noot ne why, ''unwery'', that I feynte.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 410.}}}}

'''unweary<sup>2</sup>''' (un-wē′ri), ''v. t.'' To relieve of weariness; refresh after fatigue. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|To ''unweary'' myself after my studies.
{{right|''Dryden'', Letters (ed. Malone), p. 23.}}}}

'''unweave''' (un-wēv′), ''v. t.'' '''1.''' To undo or take to pieces (that which has been woven, as a textile fabric).
{{smaller block|''Unweave'' the web of fate. ''Sandys'', Christ’s Passion, p. 4.}}
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''2.''' To separate; take apart, as the threads which compose a textile fabric.

'''unwebbed''' (un-webd′), ''a.'' Not webbed; not web-footed. ''Pennant.''

'''unwed''' (un-wed′), ''a.'' Unmarried. ''Shak.'', C. of E., ii. 1. 26.

'''unwedgeable''' (un-wej′a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not to be split with wedges; in general, not easily split; not fissile, as pepperidge. ''Shak.'', M. for M., ii. 2. 116.

'''unweeded''' (un-wē′ded), ''a.'' Not weeded; not cleared of weeds. ''Shak.'', Hamlet, ii. 1. 135.

'''unweened†''' (un-wēnd′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unwened'', < AS. ''unwēned'', unhoped; as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''weened.''] Unthought of; unexpected.
{{smaller block|Unhoped or ''unwened.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, iv. prose 6.}}}}

'''unweeping''' (un-wē′ping), ''a.'' Not weeping; not shedding or dropping tears: as, ''unweeping'' eyes. ''Drayton'', Duke Humphrey to Elenor Cobham. [Rare.]

'''unweeting†''' (un-wē′ting), ''a.'' A variant of ''unwitting.'' ''Spenser.''
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''unweeting'' Child
Shall by his beauty win his grandsire’s heart.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Vaudracour and Julia.}}}}

'''unweetingly†''' (un-wē′ting-li), ''adv.'' A variant of ''unwittingly.'' ''Milton'', S. A., l. 1680.

'''unweighed''' (un-wād′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not weighed; not having the weight ascertained.
{{smaller block|Solomon left all the vessels ''unweighed.''
{{right|1 Ki. vii. 47.}}}}
readings.c3s2:
¶
{{smaller block|Whilst they were on this discourse and pleasant tattle of drinking, Gargamelle began to be a little ''unwell.''
{{right|''Urquhart'', tr. of Rabelais, i. 6.}}
The mistress, they told us, was sick, which in America signifies what we should call being ''unwell.''
{{right|''Capt. B. Hall'', Travels in North America, I. 46.}}}}
'''2.''' As a euphemism, menstruant; having courses. Compare ''sick''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'', 6. ='''Syn. 1.''' {{smaller|''Ailing'', etc. See ''sick''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''unwellness''' (un-wel′nes), ''n.'' The state of being unwell or indisposed. ''Chesterfield'', Letter, 1755. [Rare.]

'''unwemmed†''', ''a.'' [ME., < AS. ''unwemmed;'' as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wemmed.''] Unspotted; unstained.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thus hath Crist ''unwemmed'' kept Constaunce.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Man of Law’s Tale, l. 826.}}}}

'''unwept''' (un-wept′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not wept for; not lamented; not mourned.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Unwept'', unhonoured, and unsung.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., vi. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' Not shed; not wept: as, ''unwept'' tears.

'''unwet''' (un-wet′), ''a.'' Not wet; not moist or humid; not moistened; dry.
{{smaller block|<poem>Though once I meant to meet
My fate with face unmoved and eyes ''unwet.''</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Sig. and Guis., l. 673.}}}}

'''unwhipped''' (un-hwipt′), ''a.'' Not whipped; not punished. Also ''unwhipt.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Tremble, thou wretch,
That hast within thee undivulged crimes,
''Unwhipp’d'' of justice.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iii. 2. 53.}}}}

'''unwhole†''' (un-hōl′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unhol'', ''unhal'', < AS. ''unhāl'' (= OHG. ''unhail'' = Icel. ''ūheill'' = Goth. ''unhaels''), not whole, not sound, < ''un-'', not, +
readings.c3s3:
''hāl'', whole: see ''whole.''] Not whole; not sound; infirm; unsound. ''Todd.''

'''unwholesome''' (un-hōl′sum), ''a.'' [< ME. *''unholsum, onholsom'' (= Icel. ''ūheilsamr''); < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wholesome.''] '''1.''' Not wholesome; unfavorable to health; insalubrious; unhealthful: as, ''unwholesome'' air; ''unwholesome'' food.
{{smaller block|A certaine Well . . . had once very foule water, and ''unwholesome'' to drink.
{{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 138.}}}}
'''2.''' Not sound; diseased; tainted; impaired; defective.
{{smaller block|Prithee bear some charity to my wit; do not think it so ''unwholesome.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iv. 1. 125.}}}}
'''3.''' Indicating unsound health; characteristic of or suggesting an unsound condition, physical or mental; hence, repulsive.
{{smaller block|One from whom the heart recoiled, who was offensive to every sense, with those white, ''unwholesome'', greasy hands, the powder, the scent, the masses of false hair, the still falser and more dreadful smile.
{{right|''Mrs. Oliphant'', Poor Gentleman, xliv.}}}}

'''unwholesomely''' (un-hōl′sum-li), ''adv.'' In an unwholesome manner; unhealthfully. ''The Academy'', April 12, 1890, p. 249.

'''unwholesomeness''' (un-hōl′sum-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unwholesome, in any sense; insalubrity; unhealthfulness: as, the ''unwholesomeness'' of a climate.
{{smaller block|Apulia, part of Italy, near the Adriatick gulf, where land, it seems, was very cheap, either for the barrenness and cragged heighth of the mountains or for the ''unwholesomeness'' of the air, and the wind Atabulus.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Juvenal’s Sătires, iv., note 4.}}}}

{{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I. 203.}}}}

'''unwelcome''' (un-wel′kum), ''v. t.'' To treat as being unwelcome; be displeased with. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|She can soften the occasional expression of half-concealed ridicule with which the poor old fellow’s sallies are liable to be welcomed — or ''unwelcomed.''
{{right|''The Atlantic'', LXV. 550.}}}}

'''unwelcomely''' (un-wel′kum-li), ''adv.'' In an unwelcome manner; without welcome.
{{smaller block|Garcio is come ''unwelcomely'' upon her. {{right|''J. Baillie.''}}}}

'''unwelcomeness''' (un-wel′kum-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unwelcome. ''Boyle'', Works, VI. 43.

'''unwell''' (un-wel′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not well; indisposed; not in good health; ailing; somewhat ill.

{{smaller block|Whilst they were on this discourse and pleasant tattle of drinking, Gargamelle began to be a little ''unwell.''
{{right|''Urquhart'', tr. of Rabelais, i. 6.}}
The mistress, they told us, was sick, which in America signifies what we should call being ''unwell.''
{{right|''Capt. B. Hall'', Travels in North America, I. 46.}}}}
'''2.''' As a euphemism, menstruant; having courses. Compare ''sick''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'', 6. ='''Syn. 1.''' {{smaller|''Ailing'', etc. See ''sick''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''unwellness''' (un-wel′nes), ''n.'' The state of being unwell or indisposed. ''Chesterfield'', Letter, 1755. [Rare.]

'''unwemmed†''', ''a.'' [ME., < AS. ''unwemmed;'' as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wemmed.''] Unspotted; unstained.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thus hath Crist ''unwemmed'' kept Constaunce.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Man of Law’s Tale, l. 826.}}}}

'''unwept''' (un-wept′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not wept for; not lamented; not mourned.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Unwept'', unhonoured, and unsung.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., vi. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' Not shed; not wept: as, ''unwept'' tears.

'''unwet''' (un-wet′), ''a.'' Not wet; not moist or humid; not moistened; dry.
{{smaller block|<poem>Though once I meant to meet
My fate with face unmoved and eyes ''unwet.''</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Sig. and Guis., l. 673.}}}}

'''unwhipped''' (un-hwipt′), ''a.'' Not whipped; not punished. Also ''unwhipt.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Tremble, thou wretch,
That hast within thee undivulged crimes,
''Unwhipp’d'' of justice.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iii. 2. 53.}}}}

'''unwhole†''' (un-hōl′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unhol'', ''unhal'', < AS. ''unhāl'' (= OHG. ''unhail'' = Icel. ''ūheill'' = Goth. ''unhaels''), not whole, not sound, < ''un-'', not, + ''hāl'', whole: see ''whole.''] Not whole; not sound; infirm; unsound. ''Todd.''

'''unwholesome''' (un-hōl′sum), ''a.'' [< ME. *''unholsum, onholsom'' (= Icel. ''ūheilsamr''); < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wholesome.''] '''1.''' Not wholesome; unfavorable to health; insalubrious; unhealthful: as, ''unwholesome'' air; ''unwholesome'' food.
{{smaller block|A certaine Well . . . had once very foule water, and ''unwholesome'' to drink.
{{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 138.}}}}
'''2.''' Not sound; diseased; tainted; impaired; defective.
{{smaller block|Prithee bear some charity to my wit; do not think it so ''unwholesome.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iv. 1. 125.}}}}
'''3.''' Indicating unsound health; characteristic of or suggesting an unsound condition, physical or mental; hence, repulsive.
{{smaller block|One from whom the heart recoiled, who was offensive to every sense, with those white, ''unwholesome'', greasy hands, the powder, the scent, the masses of false hair, the still falser and more dreadful smile.
{{right|''Mrs. Oliphant'', Poor Gentleman, xliv.}}}}

'''unwholesomely''' (un-hōl′sum-li), ''adv.'' In an unwholesome manner; unhealthfully. ''The Academy'', April 12, 1890, p. 249.

'''unwholesomeness''' (un-hōl′sum-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unwholesome, in any sense; insalubrity; unhealthfulness: as, the ''unwholesomeness'' of a climate.
{{smaller block|Apulia, part of Italy, near the Adriatick gulf, where land, it seems, was very cheap, either for the barrenness and cragged heighth of the mountains or for the ''unwholesomeness'' of the air, and the wind Atabulus.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Juvenal’s Sătires, iv., note 4.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
